role: Executive Secretary, California Outdoor Recreation League, Inc.
summary: Hildamae Voght, writing on behalf of the California Outdoor Recreation League, argues that the Draft Environmental Statement is inconsistent with and largely ignores the earlier ORRV Task Force Report, which recognized off-road vehicle use as a legitimate recreational activity and called for more study before imposing restrictions. She criticizes the DES for its negative and discriminatory tone toward ORV users, its failure to define 'road,' and its omission of provisions to retain off-road vehicle activity on public lands. She conditionally supports a comprehensive inventory and classification of public lands with extension of police power to all those lands, as recommended in the ORRV Report, as a fair approach to managing ORV use.

statement.text:
CALIFORNIA OUTDOOR RECREATION LEAGUE, Inc.
Non-Profit - Statewide
The United Voice For Active Outdoor Recreationists
4264 EAST FLORENCE AVENUE BELL, CALIFORNIA 90201 AREA CODE 213 - 773-6260 AREA CODE 213 - 585-0581
June 22, 1972
Department of the Interior Office of the Secretary Washington, D.C. 20240
Gentlemen:
We have the letter of June 14 from Deputy Assistant Secretary Lyons together with enclosures, and we appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Draft Environmental Statement (DES) proposed for Departmental implementation of Executive Order 11644.
We have reviewed the Off-Road Recreation Vehicle Task Force Study Report of March 15, 1972 (ORRV), and we find that the differences between that thorough study, for which we would compliment the Department and those who prepared it, and the DES difficult to reconcile.
The entire thrust of the ORRV Report is that the off-road vehicle user has a right to use and enjoy the public lands of this nation; the Report specifically recognizes the great lack of factual information (pp 42 et seq & 69, and Recommendation 8, p. 73); it specifically recommends that off-road vehicle use be recognized as an accepted recreational use and that existing use areas be kept open to the public "... where environmental balance is not at issue." (Recommendation 3, p. 70)
We would compliment the Department on this position that, in view of the need for additional study, governmental regulation should not rush blindly into the vacuum of its own ignorance with restrictions for which there is no evidence of need. We think that this is in accord with a fundamental tenet of this nation's legal system: we do not presume ever anyone's guilt.
The promise to the ear, though, was apparently only to be broken to the hope, for what was so doubtful in March evidently had become certain by May when the DES was issued. The DES could easily have been prepared without any assistance from the ORRV Report; in fact only one of the ORRV Report recommendations is included in the DES (#5), and that one is a purely restrictive one.
In March the problems with off-road vehicles were not "...as widespread or
Responsible People Working for Multiple Use of Public Lands

Department of the Interior, 6-22-72, p. ?
serious as previously thought." (ORRV 43); in May, the off-road whicle users were "...frequently in conflict with wise land and resource management practices." (DES 1) But for the fact that both the ORRV Report and the DES bore the same signature, one would almost be forced to the conclusion that this is another instance of the bureaugracy grown so large that the left hand can no longer assist in washing the right.
We note the parade of the conclusions throughout this DES as they assume themselves: "...no area of the public lands is free from potential damage..."

(13) "...use of machines...may rut slopes..." "Use of machines...

can affect..." (14) "Indiscriminate use of IRV...can have severe...
\neffects...." "...plant communities...can suffer...." "All wildlife is affected to some degree...." (15) The doubts of March are the suppositions of May.
On the other hand the "economic boom" noted by the ORRV Report (51)
"...both in the general market and in individual sections of rural America"\nin March had diminished by May to the "minor economic effects" of
controlled ORV use. (DES 17) The flowers of March plainly died in May;
the rites of Spring were brief this year.
This confusion that is so evident in the Department's turning its back on its own study less than two months after that ten-month-long study was completed is characterized, we believe, by the current term "future shock" which, though it may be excused by the arrogation of the Congressional function to the Presidential Office, is even more evident in the Secretarial directive of implementation of May 5, 1972. The Secretarial Memorandum, incorporated into this DES, adopts a definition of off-road vehicle totally at variance with the one prescribed by the Executive Order. The Presidential Proclamation made no exemption for logging trucks or construction equipment or farm tractors. Earth, in this instance, survived May, for the Secretaria, Memorandum copts the ORRV Report definition, without, however, Executive authority for doing so.
The President commands that you regulate all off-road vehicular use; you propose to requeste only off-road recreational vehicle use. The recreational vehicle user that but note his objection to this discrimination and wonder, perhaps, where in the rabbit warrens of official Washington sits this man who thinks that a motorcycle does more ecological damage than a logging truck.
We would suggest that a resolution of this difficulty, and most of the others that the implementation of Executive Order 11644 is certain to provoke, is to be found quite imply in supplying a definition of the word "road", for we are at a total loss in trying to understand how anyone can intelligently discuss "off-road" without first locating that which one shall not be permitted to get "off".

For those of us who are attempting to rise to the task of communicating in words, and to understand our lawgivers, this is the first essential.
4
Permit us, therefore, to suggest such a definition: "A road is a continuous strip of land, presently or formerly used, and suitable for use, by a vehicle."
Once this giant leap for mankind is taken, then we think your Department and its agencies can come forward with the regulations required by the Executive Order for any land use "off" the roads. It will not, of course, resolve all conflicts, but it will surely narrow them for intelligent evaluation.
We do not think even that is going to be an easy task within the assigned time limits, and especially is this so since this DES nowhere makes any provision, as the ORRV Report did, for any retention of Off-road vehicular activity, and the necessity for that is, we think, a matter of elementary fairness. The people of this land own and are entitled to use their public lands, and unless that thought is given the consideration which it deserves, your Department will be assisting in the process of transforming Executive Order 11644 into the Wilderness Act of 1972, without, mind you, even the courtesy of Congressional consultation.
We would again, as we have before, join in the ORRV Report recommendation for a comprehensive inventory and classification of the public lands and the extension of the police power to all those lands. Otherwise we, the conserving user of our public lands, must forever be called to account for, and restricted in our rights because of, the actions of the outlaw minority, the course again so patently and blindly followed by this Draft Environmental Statement.
Very truly yours,
(Mrs) Hildamae Voght Executive Secretary
